passages.t: How to carry what is holy
passages.happening:
God orders a second count of the Levites, this time of the working men ‘from thirty to fifty years old’ (verse 3). It begins with the Kohathites, whose service ‘regards the most holy things’ (verse 4).

Before the camp moves, Aaron and his sons go in first. They take down the inner curtain and cover the ark with it, then with fine leather, then with a blue cloth (verses 5-6). They wrap the table, the lampstand, the gold altar and the bronze altar in the same careful way (verses 7-14).

Only then do the Kohathites come to carry. “But they must not touch the holy objects, or they will die” (verse 15). And again: “But the Kohathites are not to go in and look at the holy objects, even for a moment, or they will die” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 3 gave each Levite clan its place. Chapter 4 is the plan for moving day. Until now the tent has stood still. Now it must travel, and the book explains with great care how the holy things can be packed and carried through a desert without harm to the men who carry them.

Sacred objects carried on poles were known in the ancient world. Egyptian priests carried images of their gods in processions, in shrines on poles, and a gilded wooden chest with carrying poles was among the objects found in the tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922. Israel's ark had the same practical form. But it held no image of God, and on the march even the gold chest itself was covered from sight.

The colors mattered. Blue and purple dyes came from sea snails, gathered in great numbers, and purple was a color of kings. Scarlet came from an insect. To wrap the furniture in such cloth was to mark it as the furniture of a king's house, even when packed for the road. Only the ark had its blue cloth on the outside, so that on the march the holiest object was the one people could pick out. The outer covering is called ‘fine leather’. The Hebrew word, tachash, is uncertain. Older English Bibles said badger skins, and some scholars think of a sea animal.

The lines were exact. Priests could see and handle the holy things. Kohathites could carry them once they were covered. Twice the passage warns of death, and the second warning is framed as mercy. God says, “Do not allow the Kohathite tribal clans to be cut off from among the Levites” (verse 18). The wrapping is done ‘in order that they may live and not die’ (verse 19). The rules are there for the sake of the men who serve.

Aaron's son Eleazar oversees the whole (verse 16).
passages.later:
The warning proved real. Centuries later the ark was moved on an ox cart, not on Levite shoulders, and a man named Uzzah died when he reached out to steady it (2 Samuel 6:6-7). David traced the disaster to neglect of this pattern: “For we did not consult Him about the proper order” (1 Chronicles 15:13). The next time, ‘the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded’ (1 Chronicles 15:15).

The curtain the priests took down in verse 5 screened the innermost room. The Gospels record that when Jesus died, “the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51). Hebrews explains that believers now ‘have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus’ (Hebrews 10:19).
passages.hard:
Why would a man die simply for touching or looking at a holy object?

The chapter says plainly that he would (verses 15 and 20), and later stories show that the warning was real (1 Samuel 6:19; 2 Samuel 6:6-7). To a modern reader this can sound like a taboo from a primitive religion, and some scholars do explain it by ancient ideas of holiness as something that spreads by contact.

Others read it as a statement about God. His holiness is not a rule he enforces from outside. It belongs to his presence, and for people who are unprepared it is dangerous in the way fire is dangerous. Read this way, the laws are a protection. God gives them so that the Kohathites ‘may live and not die’, and every death recorded later happened when the pattern was set aside.

It should be said what the passage is not. It is about one tribe's work with one set of objects in the tabernacle. It is not a picture of how God treats ordinary people who come to him in need, and it is no reason for anyone to be afraid to pray. The New Testament does not deny that God is holy. It says that Christ has opened a safe way into his presence (Hebrews 10:19-20).
passages.asks: The holy things were wrapped so that the men who carried them might live. Ask whether you have lost all sense that God is holy, so that nothing about him makes you careful. And ask whether you have the opposite trouble, a fear that keeps you from coming near, when a way has been opened.

passages.happening:
The Gershonites are counted next. “They are to carry the curtains of the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting with the covering of fine leather over it, the curtains for the entrance to the Tent of Meeting” (verse 25), with the curtains of the courtyard and their ropes (verse 26).

The sons of Merari carry ‘the frames of the tabernacle with its crossbars, posts, and bases’ (verse 31), and the posts of the courtyard with their bases, tent pegs and ropes. “You shall assign by name the items that they are responsible to carry” (verse 32).

Both clans work under Ithamar, Aaron's other son (verses 28, 33).
passages.hearers:
After the long passage on the ark, these verses can seem like a list of baggage. They are meant to be read beside it.

Every Levite between thirty and fifty had a load. The Hebrew word used for their term of duty is the word used for the army in chapters 1 and 2. The Levites were enrolled for the tent as soldiers are enrolled for a campaign. Carrying posts and rolling up curtains is given the standing of service in God's army.

The loads were assigned by name. No one had to guess what he was allowed to lift, and no item was left to chance. In a camp of this size, with a tent that had to be taken down and put up again and again for forty years, that order was a kindness.

The thirty-to-fifty age range differs from a later chapter, which sets the start of a Levite's service at twenty-five (8:24). An old Jewish explanation treats the years from twenty-five to thirty as a time of training before full service. Much later, under David, the age was lowered to twenty, because the Levites ‘no longer need to carry the tabernacle’ (1 Chronicles 23:26).
passages.later:
When Solomon's temple was built and the ark had a fixed home, the Levites' work changed. Chronicles shows them as gatekeepers, treasurers and singers (1 Chronicles 23 to 26).

Paul tells the church that the less visible parts of a body are needed too: “On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable” (1 Corinthians 12:22).
passages.asks: Each man was told by name what he was to carry. Ask what load has been given to you, in your home, your work or your church, and whether you carry it as service to God or only as a weight. And ask whether you envy someone else's load because it looks more important than yours.

passages.t: Each man his work and his burden
passages.happening:
Moses, Aaron and the leaders count the working Levites clan by clan. There are 2,750 Kohathites, 2,630 Gershonites and 3,200 Merarites, all between thirty and fifty years old. The total is 8,580 (verse 48).

The chapter ends by saying that each man was assigned ‘his work and burden’, as the LORD had commanded Moses (verse 49).
passages.hearers:
The counts are given in the same order as the commands, in nearly the same words. What God told Moses to do is then shown as done.

Of the 22,000 Levites counted in chapter 3, a little over a third are of working age. These are the men who will take down the tent, shoulder it and set it up again at each stop on the road. When the cloud lifts in chapter 10, the order of march follows these instructions exactly.

The last verse gathers the chapter into two words, work and burden. The word for burden, massa, comes from the verb to lift. It is the plain word for a load. In the prophets a word spelled the same way names a message from God. Lexicons differ on whether it is the same word, but many readers have heard in it a message laid on the prophet to carry.
passages.later: Jesus used the picture of a load when he called the weary to himself: “For My yoke is easy and My burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). This chapter does not predict that saying. It shows a world in which everyone who served God carried something, and so helps a reader hear why the words of Jesus sounded so welcome.
passages.asks: Every Levite was given both a work and a burden. Ask what you are carrying that God did not give you, a load taken up from fear or pride. And ask what it would mean, this week, to take the load Jesus offers in its place.
